problem_text: Can there be drawn on a circle of radius 1 a number of 1975 distinct points, so that the distance (measured on the chord) between any two points (from the considered points) is a rational number?
solution_text: The solution argues using chord distance formula d = 2sin(θ/2), Chebyshev polynomials preserving rationality, and placing points at vertices of a regular 1975-gon. It claims all chord distances are rational. The answer is yes. (Note: the regular 1975-gon argument is flawed since sin(πk/1975) is generally irrational. The correct method uses Pythagorean parametrization: choose 1975 rational parameters t_i with 1+t_i² a perfect square, so pairwise chord distances 2|t_i-t_j|/(q_i·q_j) are all rational.)
solution_summary: Use Pythagorean parametrization of the unit circle. For rational t with 1+t² = q² (perfect square), the point ((1-t²)/(1+t²), 2t/(1+t²)) lies on the unit circle. The chord distance between two such points with parameters t_i, t_j is 2|t_i-t_j|/(q_i·q_j), which is rational since q_i, q_j are rational. There are infinitely many Pythagorean triples, so 1975 distinct parameters can be chosen. The answer is yes.
structure_features: Existence question on continuous domain (unit circle), requiring construction of a finite set of 1975 points with pairwise rational chord distance constraint. The key structural insight is that an individual algebraic condition (1+t² = perfect square) automatically implies the pairwise condition through multiplicative closure of perfect squares.
knowledge_required: rational parametrization of unit circle via t = tan(θ/2)
key_insight: If each parameter t_i satisfies 1+t_i² = q_i² (perfect square of rational), then the product √((1+t_i²)(1+t_j²)) = q_i·q_j is automatically rational, making all pairwise chord distances rational without any pairwise compatibility check.

translation_to: algebraic parametrization (rational parameters with perfect square condition)
expected_ai_method: Regular polygon construction: place 1975 points at vertices of regular 1975-gon, incorrectly assuming sin(πk/1975) is rational for all k
correct_method: Pythagorean parametrization: choose 1975 rational parameters t_i with 1+t_i² a perfect square, ensuring all pairwise chord distances 2|t_i-t_j|/(q_i·q_j) are rational

rounds.question: Describe the structure of this problem. What formula relates the chord distance between two points on a unit circle to the central angle between them?
rounds.expected_answer: We need 1975 points on a unit circle where all pairwise chord distances are rational. The chord distance between two points subtending angle θ at the center is d = 2sin(θ/2). So we need sin(θ/2) to be rational (or more precisely, 2sin(θ/2) to be rational) for all pairwise angles.

rounds.question: List all possible approaches to construct such a set of 1975 points with pairwise rational chord distances.
rounds.expected_answer: Possible approaches: 1) Regular polygon vertices (symmetric placement), 2) Pythagorean triple parametrization of the unit circle, 3) Chebyshev polynomial approach to preserve rationality, 4) Direct construction with specific angles known to have rational sine, 5) Inductive construction adding one point at a time while maintaining rationality.

rounds.question: Try the regular 1975-gon approach. Place points at vertices of a regular 1975-gon. Does this give rational chord distances?
rounds.expected_answer: If we place points at vertices of a regular 1975-gon, the pairwise angles are 2πk/1975 for k=1,...,1974. The chord distances are 2sin(πk/1975). But sin(π/1975) is not rational in general — Niven's theorem tells us that sin(π/n) is rational only for n=1,2,6. Since 1975 is not in this set, this approach fails.

rounds.question: Instead of regular polygons, use the rational parametrization of the unit circle via t = tan(θ/2). Derive the chord distance between two points with parameters t₁ and t₂.
rounds.expected_answer: With t = tan(θ/2), a point on the unit circle is ((1-t²)/(1+t²), 2t/(1+t²)). The chord distance between points with parameters t₁ and t₂ is d = 2|t₁-t₂|/√((1+t₁²)(1+t₂²)). For this to be rational, we need √((1+t₁²)(1+t₂²)) to be rational.

rounds.question: What condition on t makes √(1+t²) rational? If each t_i satisfies this condition individually, does it automatically ensure all pairwise chord distances are rational?
rounds.expected_answer: √(1+t²) is rational when t = 2s/(1-s²) for rational s (Pythagorean triple parametrization), giving 1+t² = ((1+s²)/(1-s²))². If 1+t_i² = q_i² for each i (q_i rational), then √((1+t_i²)(1+t_j²)) = q_i·q_j is rational. So yes, the individual perfect square condition automatically ensures pairwise rationality through multiplicative closure of perfect squares.

rounds.question: How many such rational parameters t with 1+t² a perfect square exist? Can we find 1975 distinct ones?
rounds.expected_answer: There are infinitely many Pythagorean triples (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (7,24,25), ..., each giving a rational t = a/b with 1+t² = (c/b)². Since there are infinitely many, we can certainly choose 1975 distinct rational parameters t_i, each giving a distinct point on the unit circle.

rounds.question: Summarize the complete construction and confirm the answer.
rounds.expected_answer: Yes. Choose 1975 distinct rational numbers t_i such that 1+t_i² = q_i² (from Pythagorean triples). The corresponding points on the unit circle are ((1-t_i²)/(1+t_i²), 2t_i/(1+t_i²)). The chord distance between any two points i,j is 2|t_i-t_j|/(q_i·q_j), which is rational. The answer is yes.
